chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
title: King Oliver's 1929-30 Victor recordings
summary: Welburn and Moore sort out personnel and tunes for Oliver's Victor sessions, including that Moore played on 'Too Late'; Carroll Dickerson led the band.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Okay, we're talking about King Oliver now. After you made the recordings, then what?
Then we went on the road.
Okay, Oliver's band went on the road. Who was Richard Chetman? You were briefly with him, according to John Chilton here. Who was he, and what kind of...?
Moore (II) - 29
Richard Chetman. Was that a musician?
Apparently!
I can't place that name. He probably played piano, bass...
It says "Briefly with Richard Chetman's band, then toured with King Oliver late 1931 to Spring 1932." But you don't recall Chetman.
No.
Maybe we can look that up, maybe we can do something with that. But in other words, you played with Sweatman up until the time that you joined Oliver. But you made the recordings in 1929.
'29, yeah, in New York. For Victor.
For Victor, yeah. You made selections "Too Late"... No, you weren't on that; I'm sorry. "I'm Lonesome, Sweetheart," "Frankie and Johnny," "New Orleans Shout"...
They've got that thing all screwed up. I was on "Too Late."
Oh, you were on "Too Late." They have here Edmond Jones was on "Too Late," but that's you on "Too Late."
Yeah.
And "Sweet Like It Is," you were apparently on that, too.
Moore (II) - 30
Yes.
And "What Do You Want Me To Do." I guess you were on that also.
It's got "Struggle Buggy" on that?

"Struggle Buggy" was done in 1930. "Struggle Buggy" was May 22nd, 1930, with King Oliver and Dave Nelson. Well, Dave Nelson was still with the band. In fact, the band was Jimmy Archey, trombone; Bobby Holmes on clarinet and alto saxophone; Glyn Paque on alto sax; apparently Charles Frazier was on tenor; and there was Don Frye, and there was also Eric Franker on piano; the banjo player was either Arthur Taylor on most selections, it seems, or Walter Jones; and Clinton Walker was the tuba player, and you're on drums. Although you're pointing out that you were on drums on "Too Late" as opposed to Edmond Jones, who was indicated in these liner notes.
Did they have "Boogie Woogie" and "Mule Face," all them numbers?

Let's see. "Mule Face Blues," yeah. "Don't You Think I Love You, Olga," "Shake It And Break It," "Stingaree Blues" and "Nelson Stomp." Okay, so you were on all of those selections. Now, it says here... These are Martin Williams' liner notes for the Victor release, King Oliver In New York, which is a reissue on LP. It says here
Moore (II) - 31
that Carroll Dickerson was the director of the band for one of the sessions in 1930. What actually did he do?
He played violin.
Played violin. Okay...
And directed the band.
And directed the band. And King Oliver sat with the section.
Yes.
